attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed post. The quoted Ben Schmidt tweet is separate and is not part of the claim.

semantics.note: 'We don't know' X is fairly recast as 'OpenAI did not disclose' X, for the five listed categories. 'Etc.' adds nothing that can be scored.

contract.note: Reading 'architecture' and 'training data' as specific specifications rather than broad labels is an ordinary reading in the context of transparency complaints. Checking each category separately and fixing the period at launch are both fair.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous interview in which OpenAI's chief scientist confirms the parameter count and training data were not disclosed. This directly covers size and training data.

The original report gives only the 'Transformer-based' family label, which does not disclose detailed architecture. The locator points to section 2 for the withheld architecture, hardware and dataset details, but the excerpt shows only the abstract.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's chief scientist confirmed at the time that size and training data were withheld. The report gives only a broad architecture label, which under the contract does not count as disclosing architecture. No packet item shows that energy use or processor count was disclosed, and the report's stated limits on disclosure are consistent with the claim. Taken as a whole, the claim that these specifications were withheld at launch holds.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his signed post.

semantics.note: 'A bunch of commercial systems (e.g., Khan Academy)' is faithfully rendered as several systems, including Khan Academy.

contract.note: Taking 'a bunch' as several (three is enough), counting a limited pilot as adoption, and including the nonprofit the speaker himself named are all fair, ordinary readings.

evidence.note: Khan Academy's dated launch post describes a GPT-4-based Khanmigo pilot introduced that day. This is an implemented, limited adoption.
Duolingo's dated release says Duolingo Max is built on GPT-4 and available now on iOS in select markets. That is a second implemented system.

OpenAI's launch page lists Stripe, plus others, as built with GPT-4. This is a vendor disclosure, and the snapshot appears to be a later version of the page, so it is weaker corroboration of a third adopter.

reviews.rationale: At launch, Khan Academy (pilot) and Duolingo (live product) both documented implemented GPT-4 integrations. OpenAI's launch listing adds Stripe and others. That meets the contract's bar of several organisational adopters, Khan Academy included, by the time of the post.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his signed post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the Bing/GPT-4 qualifier and the 'rampant' frequency claim.

contract.note: Reading 'rampant' as 'frequent' rather than merely possible is fair. Requiring evidence of prevalence rather than isolated examples matches the word. The March 1–15 window follows reasonably from 'last week' and the present tense.

evidence.note: Reports Microsoft's confirmation that Bing ran on GPT-4. This establishes the qualifier (the condition), not the outcome.
Notes Bing was prone to hallucinations early on (before the target window) and shows one false self-description on March 14. An isolated instance does not establish frequency.
Microsoft's executive said in early March that hallucinations should decrease. This is an unquantified company statement and shows neither rarity nor frequency.

reviews.rationale: That Bing used GPT-4 is established. But the packet has no representative evaluation of how often hallucinations occurred in March 1–15, 2023. It contains one isolated error and an unquantified claim of improvement. Neither meets the support condition (frequent) or the contradiction condition (rare).

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his signed post.

semantics.note: Faithful, including the universal 'any' and the scope defined by reference to the 2022 essay.

contract.note: Defining 'solve' as dependable performance rather than benchmark gains is an ordinary reading. Taking the problem classes from the cited essay is fair, though the post does not list them itself.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own launch post concedes GPT-4 still hallucinates facts and makes reasoning errors, while also reporting improvement. This covers factuality and reasoning but not robustness to unusual inputs (outliers).
The speaker's own 2022 essay. It is used only to define scope (including outliers) and cannot serve as outcome evidence.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's own disclosure shows factual reliability and reasoning were not dependably solved at launch, so those parts of the claim are consistent with the evidence. The packet has no launch-period evaluation of robustness to unusual inputs, which the contract requires checking. Nothing shows any class was solved, but the support condition is not fully met.
